stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: For decades, ornithologists described the song repertoire of the male sedge warbler as ______: whatever phrases a male could sing by the end of his first breeding season, the thinking went, were all he would ever sing. A five-year recording study in eastern Poland now complicates that account, documenting males that added as many as a dozen new phrases during their third and fourth seasons.
explanation: The blank names the older view, and the text after the colon spells that view out: once the first season ends, the male never adds another phrase. So you need a word for a set that no longer takes anything new. "Closed" is that word. It's a plain word in a less common sense: closed to new additions. The study in the next sentence reverses the view by showing males adding phrases later in life, and that confirms the blank is about whether the repertoire can grow.

A.why: You read "by the end of his first breeding season" as "from birth." The colon says the phrases are fixed after a season of singing, which means they were acquired during that season. Nothing in the text says they are inborn, so "inherited" claims more than the description supports.

C.why: You took "all he would ever sing" to mean the repertoire is small. The colon tells you when the repertoire stops growing, not how big it is. A male with hundreds of phrases could still have a closed repertoire. "Modest" fits the topic but doesn't name what the explanation actually shows.

D.why: You chose a word that suits birdsong in general. "Repetitive" describes one male repeating the same phrases within a performance. The colon describes something else: whether he can add phrases over his lifetime. The word answers a question the text never asks.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: In her study of a Galician storyteller, folklorist Inés Varela characterizes the teller's relationship to her repertoire as ______: across forty recorded performances of a single tale, the teller reordered its episodes, renamed its characters, and moved its setting from the coast to the mountains, yet she never once altered a word of its closing riddle. Varela argues that this pattern reflects a shared understanding among the teller's listeners about which parts of a tale belong to the teller and which belong to the tradition.
explanation: The explanation after the colon has two parts, and the blank has to cover both. The teller changes almost everything, yet she keeps one part, the closing riddle, word for word. She is faithful, but only to certain parts. "Selectively faithful" names exactly that. Varela's point about which parts "belong to the tradition" confirms that the teller's loyalty is real but limited to some elements.

A.why: You saw the first insight: episodes reordered, characters renamed, setting moved. Then you stopped reading at "yet." "Freely inventive" covers only that first part. It ignores the riddle she never changed, and the colon puts that word-for-word retention at the center of the description.

C.why: You fixed on the unchanged riddle and let it stand for the whole repertoire. "Uniformly" means she treats every part the same way. The text shows the reverse: she freely reworks episodes, names, and setting.

D.why: You read the changes as memory lapses. The text gives no sign the changes are accidental. Her word-perfect recall of the riddle across forty performances points to a strong memory, and Varela explains the pattern as a shared convention, not as forgetting.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Older field guides described the foraging of the gray triggerfish as ______, and recent underwater footage complicates that description: individual fish return to the same patch of sand day after day, excavate it with the same sequence of fin strokes, and give up only after a set number of attempts.
explanation: The text after the colon describes routine: the same patch, the same sequence of strokes, a fixed number of attempts. However, that evidence is said to complicate the older label, so the blank has to name the opposite of what the footage shows. "Haphazard" means random and unplanned. The footage contradicts exactly that.

A.why: You correctly summarized the colon's evidence as "methodical," but that is what the new footage shows. The blank is the older label that the footage complicates. You named the finding instead of the view it overturns.

B.why: You matched the topic, since returning to the same patch sounds territorial. But returning to one spot supports a territorial label rather than complicating it, and the evidence is about the order of the foraging, not about defending ground.

D.why: You took the phrase "individual fish" as the point. Nothing in the footage is about whether the fish forage alone, so it can't complicate a label of "solitary."

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Silk manufacturers in eighteenth-century Lyon were celebrated for the novelty of their designs, yet the workshops' surviving pattern books reveal a striking ______: a single pomegranate motif, for example, might pass through dozens of drafts, each changing only the angle of one leaf and each annotated with a weaver's notes on how the previous draft had behaved on the loom.
explanation: "Yet" sets the blank against the workshops' reputation for novelty. The example then shows one motif changed in tiny steps, with each step responding to notes on the draft before it. "Incrementalism" means progress through small, successive adjustments, which is exactly that process.

A.why: Dozens of drafts can look inventive, but "yet" puts the blank in contrast with the reputation for novelty. Inventiveness would agree with that reputation instead of contrasting with it.

B.why: You saw many drafts and assumed the designers couldn't make up their minds. But each change was annotated in response to how the last draft behaved on the loom. That is deliberate refinement, not hesitation.

D.why: You matched the topic, since luxury silk suggests extravagance. The example shows small, careful revisions, which is the opposite of lavishness.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Collectors prize the ______ of the finest nineteenth-century Japanese woodblock prints: though a single image might require fifteen separate blocks, one for each color, printed one after another on the same sheet, the color fields in the best impressions meet without the slightest gap or overlap.
explanation: The colon explains what collectors prize. The fifteen blocks come in a "though" clause, so they are the obstacle. The prized quality comes after it: the colors meet without the slightest gap or overlap. That is exactness of alignment.

A.why: You picked a word that suits color printing in general. The evidence says nothing about how bright the colors are, only that their edges line up perfectly.

B.why: You noticed the fifteen blocks and stopped there. That detail sits in a "though" clause, which makes it the difficulty the printers overcame. What collectors prize is the result described after it.

D.why: Old paper prints may well be delicate, but nothing after the colon is about fragility. You brought in a quality the text never describes.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Forecasters along this stretch of coast call the summer sea breeze remarkably ______: its strength varies widely from one day to the next, but on nine afternoons in ten it arrives within twenty minutes of 1:00 p.m., whatever the morning's cloud cover.
explanation: The text after the colon rules out consistent strength, since the strength "varies widely." What it confirms is reliable timing: the breeze nearly always arrives within twenty minutes of 1:00 p.m. "Punctual" names reliability of timing and nothing else, so it is the only choice that fits both conditions.

A.why: You saw that the breeze is reliable and picked a general word for reliability. But a steady wind is one with constant strength, and the text says its strength varies widely.

B.why: You chose a word about wind in general. The evidence says nothing about the breeze being strong. It describes when the breeze arrives.

D.why: You stopped at "varies widely" and missed the "but" clause. The point the forecasters make is how regular the arrival time is, which is the opposite of erratic.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: To a casual observer, the narrow gaps between concrete slabs on a highway bridge may look like ______: places where the builders ran short of material or failed to line the pieces up. In fact the gaps are deliberate. Without them, slabs expanding on a hot afternoon would press against one another until the deck buckled.
explanation: The blank belongs to the casual observer's mistaken view, and the colon defines that view: builders ran short of material or failed to line the pieces up. Those are mistakes, or "oversights." The next sentence then reverses this view.

A.why: You correctly worked out what the gaps really are, but the blank is on the other side of the reversal. It names how the gaps look to a casual observer, and the colon describes that as builder error, not protection.

C.why: Nothing in the colon's description suggests decoration. You chose a word that doesn't name what the observer thinks went wrong.

D.why: Gaps are missing material, so they can't strengthen anything in the way the observer imagines. This also clashes with the colon, which describes failure rather than added support.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Economists studying the region describe its labor market as unusually ______, and they do not mean it as praise. In 2019, for example, when wages in a neighboring county rose by 15 percent, fewer than 2 percent of the region's workers changed employers, well under the national rate.
explanation: The example shows a strong signal (much higher pay nearby) that almost nobody responded to. The phrase "not ... as praise" also makes the label critical. "Inert" means failing to move or react, so it names the specific failure the example shows and carries the right negative tone.

A.why: Low turnover does look like stability, but "stable" is approving, and the text says the economists do not mean the label as praise. It also misses the point that workers ignored a clear reason to move.

C.why: You assumed a market that economists criticize must be weak or low-paying. The text never describes the region's wages or employment levels, only how little workers moved.

D.why: A competitive labor market is one where workers move toward better pay. The example shows the opposite.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: The agronomists' fertilizer recommendation is deliberately ______: rather than prescribing a single rate for every farm in the region, it tells growers to divide each field into plots, apply three different rates, and adopt whichever produced the best yield on their own soil.
explanation: The colon contrasts one regional rate with a rate each grower finds on "their own soil." The recommendation is designed to produce an answer that belongs to each farm. "Local" names that farm-by-farm quality.

A.why: Leaving out a fixed rate can look permissive. But growers are given a specific procedure to follow, so the recommendation isn't relaxing any standard.

C.why: You read testing as uncertainty. The procedure ends with growers adopting a rate, which is a firm decision. Nothing in the text suggests the agronomists are hedging.

D.why: "Rather than prescribing a single rate for every farm" rejects exactly what "uniform" describes.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: The first published report on the site dismissed its stone tools as ______. Its authors noted that nearly all were struck from a coarse local basalt and that most showed no sign of the careful edge-trimming seen elsewhere. Microscopic study of wear on the edges, however, later revealed that many had been used for fine woodworking.
explanation: The sentence right after the blank gives the report's reasons: coarse stone and no careful edge-trimming. Those reasons describe tools that are rough and unrefined, so the word is "crude." "Dismissed" confirms the label is unflattering, and the "however" sentence goes on to overturn it.

A.why: Specialized use for fine woodworking is what the later study found. The blank is the earlier dismissive view that this finding overturned, so you've put the finding on the wrong side of the reversal.

B.why: You picked up on "nearly all," which describes what the tools were made from, not how many there were. Calling tools plentiful also isn't a way to dismiss them.

D.why: The report says the basalt was local, which directly contradicts "imported."
